extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academics (at any career stage) who want to become journal peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on how to get invited to peer review for journals and how to develop the skills and visibility to be invited repeatedly. Covers building profiles, networking, training, gaining experience, and best practices for accepting and performing reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and keep updating your professional profile
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional profile is a summary of your qualifications and achievements; keep your academic CV up to date and set up profiles on services editors use so they can find you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use digital tools so editors can find you. Register for ORCiD (include your ORCID iD with submissions; ORCID lists publications and areas of interest). Set up a free profile on Web of Science and flag that you want to be a peer reviewer. Keep all profiles current, maintain university/department pages, and add links to other profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use academic and general social networks to record accomplishments and network with peers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Academia.edu and ResearchGate to add research interests, collaborations, and published work. Use LinkedIn (near-must) to promote yourself and interact professionally; general social media (Facebook, etc.) can help but are less structured for linking research. Engage regularly to increase visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Include accurate, specific keywords that match your research interests so search engines and editors can find you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add both broad and long-tail (narrow) terms (example: include “battery chemistry” and narrower terms like “lithium-ion battery anodes”). As research develops, keep keywords and profiles current; check profiles every few months and correct poorly maintained university pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Be an expert in your field to be an effective reviewer and to represent your field when a submission is not a precise match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep up to date by reading top journals, publishing research, and attending conferences and seminars. Conference presentations reveal latest findings and allow you to meet peers and editors. Continue developing research credentials and keep records updated; networking in person (or online) helps editors get to know and trust you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gain initial review experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing is a skill that requires practice; gain experience through local and informal opportunities before accepting journal reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer to help colleagues with draft articles and write short reviews; attend presentations and give constructive feedback; help your department rate internal grant proposals; volunteer to select conference abstracts; shadow a senior colleague's reviewing, write your own reviews and compare notes. Emphasize tact and tone; offer sincere, constructive advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get formal training
rubrics_metrics.description: Take formal courses or workshops to fast-track peer review skills and learn specific aspects of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for online courses (e.g., the Peer Review Power Up Course on Reviewer Credits), publisher-provided training (Elsevier, Wiley, SpringerNature), departmental or funder workshops, and mentoring programs from journals or learned societies (e.g., BMC, American Society of Agronomy). Some courses provide certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network and increase your visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Networking increases the chance editors will know and trust you and invite you to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with academic networks, research forums, and scholarly societies; present at conferences and talk to peers and editors. Meeting in person is ideal but online interactions can also build relationships and trust that make editors comfortable inviting you to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer and reach out to journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactively offer your services to journals whose scope matches your expertise to increase invitations to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify journals by where papers you cite are published and look for contact info on About or Editorial Board pages. Send a polite, concise email explaining your current research and specialist expertise. Create reviewer accounts on journal platforms when available. Ask senior colleagues to recommend you or suggest alternatives when declining invites so your name is circulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcome your first invitations, but consider them thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept every invitation automatically; evaluate invites carefully to protect your time and ensure a good match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons to decline include subject mismatch, insufficient time (allot at least 5 hours, more if inexperienced), conflicts of interest, personal circumstances, or reviewer fatigue. Read the journal’s reviewing guidelines and ensure you can fulfill the task. If in doubt, contact the editor promptly and professionally; don’t delay responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and refine your reviewing skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform reviews that balance praise with constructive criticism, help authors improve, and help editors decide about publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be reflective after each review—read it from authors' and editors' perspectives. Ensure you identify areas for improvement precisely without unduly discouraging the author. Provide clear reasons to accept/reject or concrete ideas for revisions. Learn from reviews you receive as an author and emulate best practices.
